tagline: Rainbow nation at Africa's southern tip
overview:
South Africa fills the southern end of the continent, where the cold Atlantic and warm Indian oceans meet around the Cape of Good Hope. It is about twice the size of Texas and wraps completely around the small mountain kingdom of Lesotho. Unusually, it has three capitals: Pretoria is the administrative capital, parliament sits in Cape Town, and the highest court of appeal is in Bloemfontein. Johannesburg, built on the world's richest goldfields, is the largest city.

About 60 million people live here. The country recognizes twelve official languages: eleven spoken ones, among them Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans and English, plus South African Sign Language, added in 2023. Many people switch between three or four languages in a single day. South Africa is a parliamentary republic, and its 1996 constitution is admired worldwide for its bill of rights. Mining, farming and tourism drive the economy. South Africans call their country the rainbow nation, though wide gaps between rich and poor remain from the apartheid era.
landAndNature: A high inland plateau called the highveld drops to the coast down a steep rim of mountains, the Great Escarpment, whose grandest stretch is the Drakensberg, rising above 3,400 meters. Red Kalahari sands cover the northwest, and the Karoo, a dry scrubland of flat-topped hills, fills the interior. Table Mountain stands flat above Cape Town, often draped in a cloud that locals call the tablecloth. The Cape floral kingdom is the smallest and richest of the world's plant kingdoms, with roughly 9,000 species of fynbos, most growing nowhere else. Kruger National Park, about the size of Wales, protects lions, elephants, rhinos, leopards and buffalo, and southern right whales calve along the coast each winter.
peopleAndCulture: South Africa's peoples include Zulu, Xhosa, Sotho, Tswana, Venda and Tsonga communities, descendants of Dutch and British settlers, and families of Indian, Malay and mixed heritage. A braai, or barbecue over wood coals, is a national ritual, served with boerewors sausage and pap, a maize porridge; Cape Malay curries and Durban's bunny chow, a curry served in a hollowed loaf, show the country's mixed kitchens. Soccer is the most popular sport, and South Africa hosted the 2010 World Cup; the Springboks have won the rugby World Cup four times. Gumboot dancing began in the mines, and kwaito and amapiano music came out of the townships.
history: Southern Africa holds some of the oldest human fossils, and San hunter-gatherers painted its rock shelters for thousands of years. Bantu-speaking farmers moved south about 1,800 years ago. Dutch settlers founded a supply station at the Cape in 1652, followed by British rule, wars against the Zulu kingdom and the Boer republics, and a gold and diamond rush that built Johannesburg. In 1948 the government imposed apartheid, a system of laws that separated people by race and stripped the Black majority of their rights. Protests, strikes and international pressure grew for decades, and leaders such as Nelson Mandela were imprisoned for years. Apartheid was dismantled in the early 1990s, and in 1994 all South Africans voted together for the first time, electing Mandela president.
funFacts: South Africa is the only country with three capital cities, splitting its government between Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.
The world's first successful human heart transplant was carried out in Cape Town by Christiaan Barnard in 1967.
Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison and became president four years after his release in 1990.
South Africa gave up its nuclear weapons in the early 1990s, the only country ever to dismantle an arsenal it had built.
The Cape Peninsula alone contains more plant species than the whole of Britain, and most grow nowhere else on Earth.
Table Mountain is far older than the Himalayas or the Alps, formed hundreds of millions of years ago.
